es.summary: Infección gastrointestinal causada por la bacteria C. difficile, frecuentemente asociada al uso prolongado de antibióticos y que produce diarrea acuosa y colitis.
key_points: Antibióticos alteran la flora intestinal y permiten el sobrecrecimiento de C. difficile.
Diarrea profusa y fiebre son los signos clínicos más comunes.
Se transmite por esporas en heces; requiere aislamiento de contacto.
El tratamiento de primera línea incluye vancomicina oral o fidaxomicina.
Complicaciones graves: colitis pseudomembranosa, megacolon tóxico y sepsis.

pathophysiology: Los antibióticos destruyen la microbiota protectora del colon.
C. difficile produce toxinas A y B que dañan la mucosa colónica.
El daño mucoso genera inflamación y secreción de líquido, provocando diarrea.
risk_factors: Uso de antibióticos > 7 días (esp. clindamicina, cefalosporinas).
Estancia hospitalaria o residencia de ancianos.
Uso de inhibidores de bomba de protones.
diagnostics: Técnica de detección de toxina en heces (ELISA) o PCR para genes de toxina.
Imagen: radiografía abdominal para descartar megacolon tóxico.
treatment: Vancomicina oral 125 mg cada 6 h (primer línea).
Metronidazol solo si no hay disponibilidad de vancomicina oral.
Reposición de líquidos y electrolitos por vía oral o IV.
Probiotics pueden considerarse para prevenir recurrencia.
nursing_care: Evaluar frecuencia, volumen y características de las deposiciones.
Monitorear signos vitales cada 4 h; prestar atención a fiebre y taquicardia.
Registrar ingesta y salida de líquidos; mantener balance hídrico.
Aplicar aislamiento de contacto: guantes y bata al entrar/salir de la habitación.
Educar al personal sobre desinfección de superficies con lejía al 1 %.
patient_teaching: Lavado de manos con agua y jabón o alcohol gel antes y después de usar el baño.
Mantener la habitación bien ventilada y limpiar superficies con desinfectante aprobado.
Informar al médico si la diarrea persiste > 3 días o aparecen sangre en heces.
Evitar el uso innecesario de antibióticos y preguntar al médico antes de tomarlos.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de déficit de volumen de líquidos
outcomes: Balance hídrico: mantener ingesta y salida de líquidos dentro de ±500 mL/24 h.
Peso corporal: permanecer estable (variación < 0.5 kg en 48 h).

interventions.action: Monitorear ingesta y salida de líquidos cada 8 h.
interventions.rationale: Detectar rápidamente déficit hídrico y guiar la reposición.

interventions.action: Evaluar signos de deshidratación (turgor, mucosas, presión arterial).
interventions.rationale: Identificar deterioro antes de que se produzca shock.

interventions.action: Administrar solución de rehidratación oral o IV según prescripción.
interventions.rationale: Reemplazar pérdidas de agua y electrolitos.

interventions.action: Registrar peso diario y comparar con peso basal.
interventions.rationale: Controlar la tendencia de pérdida o ganancia de peso.

interventions.action: Informar al médico si el balance hídrico es negativo > 500 mL/24 h.
interventions.rationale: Permite ajuste oportuno de la terapia de fluidos.

outcomes: Electrolitos séricos: mantener potasio 3.5‑5.0 mEq/L y sodio 135‑145 mEq/L.
No presentar arritmias relacionadas con alteraciones electrolíticas.

interventions.action: Obtener panel de electrolitos cada 24 h mientras persista la diarrea.
interventions.rationale: Detectar desequilibrios tempranos.

interventions.action: Evaluar signos neuromusculares (calambres, debilidad).
interventions.rationale: Los síntomas pueden indicar hipopotasemia o hiponatremia.

interventions.action: Administrar suplementos de potasio o sodio según orden médica.
interventions.rationale: Corregir déficits y prevenir complicaciones cardíacas.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre alimentos ricos en potasio (plátano, papaya).
interventions.rationale: Apoyo dietético para mantener niveles adecuados.

interventions.action: Monitorear ritmo cardíaco y presión arterial cada 4 h.
interventions.rationale: Identificar arritmias inducidas por desequilibrios electrolíticos.

en.summary: Gastrointestinal infection caused by the bacterium C. difficile, frequently associated with prolonged antibiotic use and producing watery diarrhea and colitis.
key_points: Antibiotics alter intestinal flora and allow overgrowth of C. difficile.
Profuse diarrhea and fever are the most common clinical signs.
It is transmitted by spores in feces; requires contact isolation.
First‑line treatment includes oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin.
Severe complications: pseudomembranous colitis, toxic megacolon, and sepsis.

pathophysiology: Antibiotics destroy the protective microbiota of the colon.
C. difficile produces toxins A and B that damage colonic mucosa.
Mucosal damage causes inflammation and fluid secretion, leading to diarrhea.
risk_factors: Hospital stay or nursing home residency.
diagnostics: Stool toxin detection by ELISA or PCR for toxin genes.
Imaging: abdominal X‑ray to rule out toxic megacolon.
treatment: Oral vancomycin 125 mg every 6 h (first line).
Metronidazole only if oral vancomycin unavailable.
Rehydration and electrolyte replacement orally or IV.
Probiotics may be considered to prevent recurrence.
nursing_care: Assess frequency, volume, and characteristics of stools.
Monitor vital signs every 4 h; watch for fever and tachycardia.
Record intake and output; maintain fluid balance.
Apply contact isolation: gloves and gown when entering/exiting the room.
Educate staff on surface disinfection with 1 % bleach.
patient_teaching: Wash hands with soap and water or alcohol gel before and after using the bathroom.
Keep the room well ventilated and clean surfaces with approved disinfectant.
Notify the physician if diarrhea persists > 3 days or blood appears in stool.
Avoid unnecessary antibiotic use and ask the physician before taking them.

outcomes: Fluid balance: maintain intake and output within ±500 mL/24 h.
Body weight: remain stable (variation < 0.5 kg in 48 h).

interventions.action: Monitor intake and output every 8 h.
interventions.rationale: Detect fluid deficit early and guide replacement.

interventions.action: Assess signs of dehydration (turgor, mucous membranes, blood pressure).
interventions.rationale: Identify deterioration before shock.

interventions.action: Administer oral or IV rehydration solution as prescribed.
interventions.rationale: Replace water and electrolyte losses.

interventions.action: Record daily weight and compare with baseline weight.
interventions.rationale: Track trend of weight loss or gain.

interventions.action: Notify the physician if fluid balance is negative > 500 mL/24 h.
interventions.rationale: Allows timely adjustment of fluid therapy.

outcomes: Serum electrolytes: maintain potassium 3.5‑5.0 mEq/L and sodium 135‑145 mEq/L.
No arrhythmias related to electrolyte disturbances.

interventions.action: Obtain electrolyte panel every 24 h while diarrhea persists.
interventions.rationale: Detect early imbalances.

interventions.action: Assess neuromuscular signs (cramps, weakness).
interventions.rationale: Symptoms may indicate hypokalemia or hyponatremia.

interventions.action: Administer potassium or sodium supplements as ordered.
interventions.rationale: Correct deficits and prevent cardiac complications.

interventions.action: Educate patient on potassium‑rich foods (banana, papaya).
interventions.rationale: Dietary support to maintain adequate levels.

interventions.action: Monitor heart rhythm and blood pressure every 4 h.
interventions.rationale: Identify arrhythmias induced by electrolyte imbalances.

summary.0.quote: C. diff is a bacterium that can cause diarrhea and more serious intestinal conditions such as colitis.

key_points.1.quote: The symptoms of C. diff infections include: Diarrhea (loose, watery stools) or frequent bowel movements for several days Fever Stomach tenderness or pain Loss of appetite Nausea Severe diarrhea causes you to lose a lot of fluids.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: You are at more likely to get a C. diff infection if you: Are taking antibiotics Are 65 or older Recently stayed in a hospital or nursing home Have a weakened immune system Have had a previous infection with C.

sections.complications.0.quote: C. diff Infections Also called: Clostridioides difficile infections, Clostridium difficile Infections, Clostridium enterocolitis, Pseudomembranous colitis

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: Wash your hands with soap and water after you use the bathroom and before you eat.
